fields.label: Panels ×9
rows: Ethylene propylene diene rubber, the default for water, steam, coolant and weather-exposed joints, with excellent ozone and UV resistance. The compound most gasket enquiries end up specifying. Not for petroleum oils.

Nitrile butadiene rubber, the general-purpose industry standard. Outstanding resistance to petroleum oils and hydraulic fluids at moderate temperature, which makes it the usual choice for oil-side flange and housing joints.
Fluorocarbon rubber, the first choice for aggressive chemical environments. Resists petroleum oils, fuels and many solvents at sustained high temperature, and holds a joint where NBR would harden.

Vinyl methyl silicone, the widest service range of the eight. Specified for enclosure, lighting and oven-side gaskets. Food-contact and biocompatible grades on request. Poor abrasion resistance — not a wear part.

Ethylene acrylic elastomer. Our signature compound, supplied to Mahindra & Mahindra for engine and transmission applications. Holds compression-set stability where oil, heat and ozone act together — the condition that ends most cover-joint gaskets.
Polychloroprene. Balanced across weather, refrigerants and moderate oil exposure, and the family we reach for when flame retardancy is specified. Common on HVAC and refrigerant-line joints.
Styrene butadiene rubber. Abrasion resistance at low cost, for static joints in water and mild service. Not for oil or fuel contact.
Polyisoprene. The highest resilience of the eight, specified where a gasket also has to damp or take repeated closing loads. Not for oil, fuel or sustained heat.

Closed-cell expanded EPDM to ASTM D1056, classified by type, class and grade rather than Shore hardness — the grade sets the force needed for 25% compression deflection. Specified where a joint has to seal against a large gap or an uneven face, as on C-pillar garnish and cabinet doors.
fields.note: Nine panels. Panel order leads with EPDM, NBR and FKM because those three cover most gasket service; the live order leads with FKM, which is the least commonly specified of the three. Every range matches the homepage compound table, which governs across all eleven category pages. Body copy for the four live panels is kept close to the original where it is accurate — only the numbers change, plus a “not for” clause on EPDM and a service note on each

Heading levels. The section heading is <h2>; each compound name is <h3> inside the panel. Nine <h3>s under one question <h2> is a clean, extractable outline.
The H2 is a literal buyer question, which is the AEO pattern. The passage under it should answer in the first 40 to 60 words, before the accordion starts — which is what the rewritten intro does.

Hardness for the sponge panel is not a Shore A band. ASTM D1056 classifies cellular rubber by type, class, suffix and grade, where the grade is the force for 25% compression deflection. Publishing a Shore A figure there would be a category error, so the field carries the classification instead.
